sections.title: Listening
sections.content:
Part 1 — Transcript

IELTS Listening You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four sections.

Write all your answers in the listening question booklet. At the end of the test, you will be given 10 minutes to transfer your answers to an answer sheet.

Now turn to section 1 on page 2 of your question booklet.

Section 1 You will hear a man phoning a community center to find out about the programs they run.

First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6 on page 2. You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first. Good afternoon. Watertown Community Center registration desk. Maria speaking. Oh, good afternoon. I'm calling about registering my family in some of your programs.

The name of the person on the registration desk is Maria. So, Maria has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6.

Good afternoon. Watertown Community Center registration desk. Maria speaking. Oh, good afternoon. I'm calling about registering my family in some of your programs. Certainly. Which ones? Well, let's start with me. I want to take a yoga class. Can you tell me about the different classes you offer? Well, our modern yoga class is great if you're looking for a real workout or if you want to get rid of some excess weight.

You'll definitely sweat in this class. Sounds good. Our Yoga and More class combines the best of yoga and Pilates to help strengthen a person's core muscles. Would it help me with my sore back? Yes. A lot of people find it helps.

We also have our original yoga class. If you're more advanced, I wouldn't recommend it, but it's a good choice for beginners. Thanks. How long are the classes? Uh, the classes used to be 45 minutes long, but we've added 10 minutes of relaxation at the end this year, so the classes are 55 minutes long. Is there anything I need to bring?

We provide towels if you want to have a shower afterwards, but for the class you'll need to bring your own mat. Okay, sounds good. Can I help you with anything else? Yes. What about ballet classes? My daughter loves ballet, and she's done it for six years.

Well, then we've got some advanced classes. We offer a class on Wednesdays. It concentrates on complicated routines and jumps. We also have a class on Thursdays, which your daughter could possibly do as well. She would have to try out for it because they're getting ready for a competition.

Okay, I'll let her know.

Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten on page two.

Now listen and answer questions seven to ten. Now, anything else? Yes. My son wants to play soccer. He's never done it before. Our rookies team would be a perfect fit for him. We don't focus on rules. We just try to help children develop the basic skills in a fun way.

Okay, what day is that? Uh, they play on Thursdays at five. Does that work for you? Yes, that's perfect. Do I need to provide anything? Does he need his own ball? No, that's all taken care of. Oh, we do request the parents take turns providing a snack for the team to share at halftime.

You'll be given a schedule for when it's your turn. Okay. Great. Are you interested in anything else? Actually, yes. My wife wanted me to ask you about your aerobics classes. Yes, we have them 16 times a week at various times. The evening classes are really popular,

so I'd recommend she come before she starts work if she can. Are all the aerobics classes the same? We have many different classes. For example, some emphasize using weights to improve muscle tone. In other classes, they really work on high-impact aerobics to keep the heart strong. Okay. Can I register my family? My name's Bob Hanson.

Okay, I've signed your family up, so your registration will be held for 24 hours, okay? Yes. How do I pay? I can't take payment over the phone. You can pay for this online by credit or debit card, or you can pay at reception. Okay. I'd like to pay in person. Can I get a tour of the facilities while I'm there?

Yes. Come by during business hours. The cost will be $360 for your entire family for 12 weeks. You've been most helpful. Thanks. You're welcome. Bye.

That is the end of section one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

Part 2 — Transcript

Now turn to section two on page three. Section two. You will hear a podcast about a famous park in Canada. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14 on page three.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good afternoon, and welcome to this podcast about Royal Nature Park. It's a historical park in Canada that was home to the First Nations people and early settlers many years ago. First Nations groups settled in this area around a lake over 600 years ago, and the discovery of corn residue at the lowest level of the lake led scientists to believe that corn was once cultivated in the

area by the First Nations people. This lake, now in the center of the park, has varying depths and temperatures. Parts of the lake are so deep that there is virtually no oxygen and sunlight. This means that plants and fish have trouble surviving there. The only natural residents of the lake are large turtles that lie on rocks or at the lake edge. Visitors are asked not to swim in the lake so as not to disturb them, but it's fine to take photos of them.

The park has a replica of a First Nations village from long ago. This includes three reconstructed longhouses where families live together. We built them based on pictures and findings to resemble the ones from over 600 years ago. They're called longhouses mainly for their shape. They're long but not tall and have benches on both sides of the house that are used as beds. The people used furs from animals to keep warm at night, and they built fire pits inside for

warmth and cooking, especially during the winter. The houses often were home for a number of families. All members of the families helped to build the house and contributed to the daily work, including children. Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20 on page 4. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. There are many things to do and see during the year at Royal Nature Park. During the spring,

treat your taste buds to an event called Sweet Water Season, the sweetest festival here at the park. Find out how the early settlers removed the liquid called sap from the maple trees. They boiled it into a thick syrup that they used to sweeten food. Samples are available for those who wish to taste it. A favourite event is our Season of the Harvest programme.

Gather apples from the trees and join us in the fields as we harvest pumpkins, beans and potatoes. Early settlers relied on these crops for the winter. You can even purchase some of the fresh fruit and vegetables in the gift shop. Join the Fall Into Nature Festival for a special live viewing of hawks and other birds of prey. During the display, watch our trained staff work with these creatures in their natural habitat.

Visitors can have the thrill of a wild bird landing on their arm. Our Moccasin Time event is held every four weeks at the time of the full moon. It starts at 11pm and it takes an hour to cover the park on foot, so you'll need to bring a flashlight. If you listen carefully, you may be able to hear the owls calling to each other as they hunt for food in the dark. In September, try the Hide and Seek Trail.

Take it towards the lake and you'll see some sculptures cut into old trees and logs with a knife. These represent the wildlife of the area, including bears, birds and reptiles, which are rapidly disappearing. See if you can identify the animal in each sculpture. In the snowy season, join a group and try cross-country skiing on Pine Ridge Way. You'll head through frosted pine trees and over snow-covered hills. There are many paths for you

to choose from. Look out for the arrows on trees to get back to the visitor's center and get warm.

That is the end of section 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

Part 3 — Transcript

Now turn to section 3 on page 5. Section 3. You will hear two researchers comparing their research on different types of bees. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25 on page 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25. Have you had a chance to look at our research on Australian native bees? Yes, it's very relevant to my research on European bees.

What aspect do you think is most relevant? Well, as you know, my main research interest is the European honey bee and the problems facing it. Yes, I've heard about the varroa mite, but I don't know much about it. Well, it almost wiped out the European honey bee population in North America back in the 1980s. Thankfully, we don't have it here in Australia yet. It sounds like a nasty little creature.

It certainly is. It's like a little hitchhiker, really. It hops onto a bee, then when the bee lands on a flower, the mite gets off and waits for another bee to come along. And from there, I guess the mite climbs onto another bee. Right. The mite then hitches a ride back to the hive where the bee lives with the rest of the colony. So the mite actually sneaks inside the hive on top of the bee's back.

That's right. And once it's there, it dives into a honeycomb cell and heads straight for the bottom. That's where the queen bee's eggs are. And the honey. Yes. And the mite buries itself deep inside it. Ah, I see. The mite doesn't eat the honey, though, does it?

Well, no. That's the interesting part. It uses the honey to cover its scent, so it won't be detected. And presumably, it lives off the blood of the bees. That's right. It feeds on the bee larva that hatches out from the egg. The mite's reproductive cycle takes place there, too, while it's living in the cell.

When that's finished, it leaves. It sounds like a clever enemy. But why does it have such a devastating effect on bee populations? Well, it leaves them debilitated, and it also infects them with a virus that spreads amongst the colony. If the population dies out here in Australia, it will have a devastating effect on Australian

agriculture. The worrying thing is that we do need to find a way of increasing our bee population.

Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30 on page 6. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30. Well, perhaps we can combine my research on European bees and yours on Australian native bees to put together a research proposal and find a way of safely increasing the Australian bee population.

That would be great. Let's compare notes. Okay, then. Let's start with the European bumblebee. There's been a lot of talk recently about bringing them into this country. Yes, but the problem is that the bumblebee has a tendency to carry weeds to nearby farmland. They would also compete for nectar with your existing bees.

You know, there's an Australian native bee, the blue banded bee, which is good at pollinating without carrying weeds. It could be useful to farmers. The blue banded bee? I've never heard of that one. That's one of the challenges we face because there hasn't been a lot of research on it as yet.

Well, it's better to use native bees because importing them can be disastrous. The Africanised bees are case in point. It was introduced into South America because it was a good honey producer, but what they didn't realise was that it attacks anything that moves. Speaking of honey producers, the Australian stingless bee is a good alternative source of honey.

Oh, I didn't know they produced honey. Yes, although they don't produce as much as other bees do. The main drawback with the stingless bees is that they're quite sensitive to temperature. They just won't fly if it gets below 18 degrees, so they aren't really suited to southern parts of Australia.

I know how you feel about foreign bees, but I think my favourite bee is a Canadian leafcutter bee. It has such a gentle personality, but it's really hard working too and it's got a lot of potential for farmers. Why is that? Well, I've been asked to help import them to this country to pollinate the lucerne or alfalfa

crops. At the moment, Australian production is about a third of that in North America, where they have these leafcutter bees. That's quite a difference, but is it safe to import these bees? Well, our research shows that it is, so they've been importing them in very limited numbers. They have to be thoroughly checked first before they're released to make sure that

they don't have any mites or diseases. Well, that's good. Yes. Of course, the only drawback is that we can't bring in very many at a time, so we still don't have enough of them here to really make much difference to our crop yields. Yes, it takes time to build up a bee population.

That is the end of section 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

Part 4 — Transcript

Now turn to section 4 on page 7.

Section 4. You will hear an expert giving a lecture to business students about how to review a project.

First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on page 7.

Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. In the last lecture, we looked at managing a project to completion. Today, we're going to be looking at a way of judging just how successful your project has been. It's called the after-action review process. A typical project review is completed long after the project is finished,

and so it's too late to change the outcome. Wouldn't it be better to evaluate it along the way so you can learn from your mistakes at each stage and improve on them? It was for this reason that the Army devised the after-action review process as a way for everyone to learn quickly from experiences in the field.

Okay, so what are the benefits of using an after-action review? Firstly, it's not just limited to very large or very formal projects, but is useful for all sorts of things. For example, you may want to use it to debrief following a staff meeting or any other regular operational function.

In the same manner, it's an extremely effective tool to use following a safety incident and can reveal important lessons so that accidents can be avoided in the future. So you can see that this would definitely be a positive step for any business. An added benefit of the review is that because the focus is on learning, it really improves communication within working groups.

So let's have a look at what an after-action review is. It's a structured session or meeting that does the following. It focuses on the resulting outcomes and the reasons for these. It encourages active participation among the team and, very importantly, emphasises how vital it is for the team to trust one another.

Here are some of the key elements to remember for when you're conducting an after-action review. Where possible, it's really good to have an external person to facilitate the process. This helps to direct the discussion and can also prevent a stronger member of the review from dominating the others. Make sure that you encourage active involvement.

Often, shy members won't say anything, so one way to encourage them to get involved is to ask people to put their comments in writing. If they aren't given the opportunity to do this, they may be intimidated by other members of the group. Another key element is to be aware of the type of questions you ask.

In order to make sure that participants don't search for what they think is the perfect answer, always ask open questions. For example, what would you do differently next time? Ensure that every member of the team has the chance to speak. It's also important to make sure you write down the specific recommendations made by everyone.

But don't forget to pass this information on to non-participating team leaders so that they too can learn from the experience. This is how after-action reviews contribute to organisation-wide learning and improvement. However, if no one follows up on these recommendations, then the process is wasted. You should also ensure that the ideas from the after-action review

are incorporated into your business by organising staff training around them. Finally, the last thing you want is to find that you don't get through everything because you've been talking too much, so make sure you keep a constant eye on the time. An after-action review is not something that you should ever plan on conducting in two sessions. Now, before we go on to look at the next type of project review,

the PIP, post-implementation review, are there any questions?

That is the end of section 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

That is the end of the listening test.

sections.title: Reading
sections.content:
READING PASSAGE 1

Herding

Many animals naturally live and travel together in groups called herds as a form of protection against predators. They move from one fertile grassland to another without an organized direction. Herding is the practice of caring for these roaming groups of livestock over a large area. Herding developed about 10,000 years ago, as prehistoric hunters domesticated wild animals such as cows and goats. Hunters learned that by controlling animals they once pursued, they could have reliable sources not only of meat, but also of milk and milk products, as well as animal hides for tents and clothing.

There are several different types of herding. One of the most ancient forms is nomadic herding, which involves tribal or extended-family groups moving with their animals from one grazing area to another. Nomads live in arid and semi-arid parts of Africa, Asia and Europe, and in the tundra regions of Asia and Europe, where land is not fertile enough for intensive agricultural farming. In Africa, nomadic tribes herd various animals such as cattle, goats, sheep and camels. The Fulani people of Nigeria are a typical example: their animals are used for producing milk and are rarely slaughtered for meat. In the polar tundra, in the northernmost part of Europe, nomads usually herd domesticated reindeer, horses, musk-oxen and yaks.

Nomadic herding is sometimes considered a form of subsistence agriculture. However, unlike subsistence farmers, herders are traditionally wage-earners: they sell their herds’ materials for goods and services, or herd other people’s animals for a fee. Often, this trade is part of the informal economy, not accounted for by the government of a region. In Africa, the United Nations estimates that herders are responsible for more than $100 million in economic activity every year.

Nomadic herding as a way of life is declining because of natural disasters, loss of land area due to development, and climate change, as well as pressure from governments to lead a settled existence. Permanent residence allows members of a nomadic community to have access to education and healthcare facilities. However, the complex social structure of herding communities is lost as they are absorbed into mainstream culture. The unique language and customs of nomads become redundant in settled urban or suburban life.

Another form of herding is semi-nomadic herding. These herders live a more settled life than nomads, but many still follow their herds for long periods of time. Prior to the 20th century, the Bedouin people of the Arabian Peninsula and the Middle East were mostly nomads, herding sheep and goats. However, recurring drought throughout Western Asia in the 1960s limited fertile areas; plus oil production in Egypt and Saudi Arabia further limited land available for grazing. Bedouins are now almost entirely semi-nomadic or settled.

Today, about a quarter of Mongolia’s population continues to live a semi-nomadic herding lifestyle, herding sheep, goats, horses and camels. However, young people have recently been rejecting this way of life and are instead moving to the city in search of an easier life.

The Sami are semi-nomadic herders indigenous to the Arctic. They live throughout northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and on the Kola Peninsula of Russia. For centuries, the Sami have herded reindeer as a principal means of livelihood, supplemented by fishing and trapping. Land development has made it difficult for these semi-nomadic herders to sustain their traditional way of life. State and national borders, for example, have divided traditional Sami land. Trees are also being cut down for the timber industry, and mines dug to extract minerals, which is all having a serious impact on grazing land. There are laws to protect the Sami and their grazing rights, but conflicts still exist.

Another type of herding in mountainous regions is called transhumance. Transhumance herders follow a seasonal migration pattern, usually to highlands in the summer and lowlands in the winter. Unlike nomads, these herders move their animals between the same areas, and live in fixed settlements.

Transhumance has had an enormous impact on the landscape. In the European Alps, for instance, thousands of years of transhumance have transformed forests into grassland. Swiss and German herders traditionally led sheep, cattle and pigs to pastures at elevations above 2,000 meters.

Transhumance in the Alps has traditionally involved three herding grounds. The lowest elevation is where livestock are kept sheltered during the cold and snowy winter months. Shepherds lead herds to the middle pastures during the spring. During the summer and fall, shepherds lead sheep and cattle to the highest pastures, while pigs are kept in the middle area. Transhumance is still widely practised throughout agricultural areas in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Italy and Slovenia.

READING PASSAGE 2

The conquest of malaria in Italy

A review of Frank M Snowden's masterly history of a country's fight to eradicate a deadly disease

A The word 'malaria' means 'bad air' in Italian, and this terrible disease marked the life of the people of that country for thousands of years. Yet by 1962, Italy was officially declared malaria-free, and it has remained so ever since. Frank Snowden's study of this successful endeavour is a remarkable piece of historical work. Original, crystal clear, analytical and passionate, Snowden takes us to areas historians have rarely visited before.

B Everybody now knows that malaria is carried by mosquitoes. But in the 19th century most experts subscribed to the theory of 'miasma' or 'poisoning of the air'. Others made a link between swamps, water and malaria, but did not make the further leap towards insects. The consequence of these theories was that little was done to combat the disease before the end of that century. The situation was so serious that from a total population of 25m Italians, 11m were 'permanently at risk'. In warm, damp, malarial zones, the life expectancy of land workers was a terrifying 22.5 years. The economic impact of the disease was immense. Epidemics were blamed on people who originated from the hotter parts of Italy, given the widespread belief that malaria was hereditary.

C One of the first breakthroughs in the war against malaria came in 1898 when the zoologist Giovanni Battista Grassi demonstrated that the micro-organisms causing the disease were carried in the digestive tract of the mosquito. By releasing mosquitoes into rooms to drink the blood of healthy human volunteers, Grassi was able to make the direct link between the insects and the disease. Definitive proof of this theory was obtained after an extraordinary series of experiments in Italy, where healthy people were introduced into malarial zones but kept free of mosquito bites - and remained well. The recently formed Italian state at last had the necessary information to begin tackling the disease.

D A complicated approach was adopted, which made use of quinine - a drug obtained from tree bark which had long been used to combat fever, but was now seen as a crucial part of the war on malaria. Italy introduced a quinine law and a quinine tax in 1904, and the drug was administered to large numbers of rural workers. Despite its often terrible side effects, the drug was successful in limiting the spread of the disease, and in breaking cycles of infection. In addition, Italy set up rural health centres and invested heavily in education programmes. Malaria, as Snowden shows, was not just a medical problem, but a social and regional issue, and could only be defeated through multi-layered strategies.

E It was originally decided to give quinine to all those in vulnerable regions - even healthy people. However, peasants were often suspicious of medicine being forced upon them, and doctors were frequently met with hostility and stubborn refusal to accept the treatment offered. But despite the refusals, the strategy as a whole was hugely successful. Deaths from malaria fell by some 80% in the first decade of the 20th century and some areas escaped altogether from the scourge of the disease.

F The 1915-18 war delayed the campaign, as funds were diverted to the battlefields. In the 1920s and 1930s the draining of the damp, unhealthy marshlands around Rome had a certain impact on the spread of malaria. However, as war swept through the drained lands in the 1940s, the disease returned with a vengeance. Yet the country's leading malariologist Alberto Missiroli refused to order the distribution of quinine, so allowing the epidemic to spread unchecked. According to Snowden, he did this in order to create the ideal conditions for a new strategy, supported by the US Rockefeller Foundation - a massive experiment involving the extermination of mosquitoes with the chemical DDT. It is estimated that more than a third of the inhabitants in the affected area contracted malaria and countless thousands died.

G With the end of the war in 1945, the US government and the Rockefeller Foundation were free to experiment. DDT was sprayed from the air, and 3m Italians had their bodies covered with the chemical. The effects were immense, and by 1962 malaria was more or less gone from the whole country. One of the final victims to die of the disease in Italy was the popular cyclist, Fausto Coppi. He had contracted malaria in Africa in 1960, and the failure of doctors in Italy to spot the disease was a sign of the times. A few decades earlier, they would have immediately noticed the telltale signs; it was later claimed that a small dose of quinine would have saved his life.

H As there are still more than 1m deaths every year from malaria worldwide, Snowden's book also has contemporary relevance. This is a disease that affects every level of the societies where it is rampant. The economic miracle of the 1950s and 1960s which made Italy into a modern industrial nation would not have been possible without the eradication of malaria. Moreover, this book convincingly argues that the disease was 'an integral part of the big picture of modern Italian history'. This magnificent study, beautifully written and impeccably documented, deserves an audience beyond specialists in history, or in Italy.

READING PASSAGE 3

The significant role of mother tongue language in education

One consequence of population mobility is an increasing diversity within schools. To illustrate, in the city of Toronto in Canada, 58% of kindergarten pupils come from homes where English is not the language of communication. Schools in Europe and North America have experienced this diversity for years, but educational policies and practices vary widely between countries and even within countries. Some political parties and groups search for ways to “solve the problem of diverse communities and their integration in schools and society.” They see few positive consequences for the host society and worry that diversity threatens the identity of the host society. Consequently, they promote unfortunate educational policies that will make the “problem” disappear. If students retain their culture and language, they are viewed as less capable of identifying with the mainstream culture and learning the mainstream language of the society.

The challenge for educators and policymakers is to shape the evolution of national identity in such a way that the rights of all citizens (including school children) are respected, and the cultural, linguistic and economic resources of the nation are maximized. To waste the resources of the nation by discouraging children from developing their mother tongues is quite simply unintelligent from the point of view of national self-interest. A first step in providing an appropriate education for culturally and linguistically diverse children is to examine what the existing research says about the role of children’s mother tongues in their educational development.

In fact, the research is very clear. When children continue to develop their abilities in two or more languages throughout primary school, they gain a deeper understanding of language and how to use it effectively. They have more practice in processing language, especially when they develop literacy in both. More than 150 research studies conducted during the past 35 years strongly support what Goethe, the famous eighteenth-century German philosopher, once said: that the person who knows only one language does not truly know that language. Research suggests that bilingual children may also develop more flexibility in their thinking as a result of processing information through two different languages.

Children who come to school with a solid foundation in their mother tongue develop stronger literacy abilities in the school language. When parents and other caregivers (e.g., grandparents) are able to spend time with their children and tell stories or discuss issues with them in a way that develops their mother tongue, children come to school well-prepared to learn the school language and succeed educationally. Children’s knowledge and skills transfer across languages from the mother tongue to the school language. Transfer across languages can be two-way—both languages nurture each other when the educational environment permits children access to both languages.

Some educators and parents are suspicious of mother tongue-based teaching programs because they worry that they take time away from the majority language. For example, in a bilingual program where 50% of the time is spent teaching through children’s home language and 50% through the majority language, surely children won’t progress as far in the latter? One of the most strongly established findings of educational research, however, is that well-implemented bilingual programs can promote literacy and subject matter knowledge in a minority language without any negative effects on children’s development in the majority language. Within Europe, the Foyer program in Belgium, which develops children’s speaking and literacy abilities in three languages (their mother tongue, Dutch and French), most clearly illustrates the benefits of bilingual and trilingual education (see Cummins, 2000).

It is easy to understand how this happens. When children are learning through a minority language, they are learning concepts and intellectual skills too. Pupils who know how to tell the time in their mother tongue understand the concept of telling time. In order to tell time in the majority language they do not need to re-learn the concept. Similarly, at more advanced stages, there is transfer across languages in other skills, such as knowing how to distinguish the main idea from the supporting details of a written passage or story, and distinguishing fact from opinion. Studies of secondary school pupils are providing interesting findings in this area, and it would be worth extending this research.

Many people marvel at how quickly bilingual children seem to pick up conversational skills in the majority language at school (although it takes much longer for them to catch up with native speakers in academic language skills). However, educators are often much less aware of how quickly children can lose their ability to use their mother tongue, even in the home context. The extent and rapidity of language loss will vary according to the concentration of families from a particular linguistic group in the neighborhood. Where the mother tongue is used extensively in the community, then language loss among young children will be less. However, where language communities are not concentrated in particular neighborhoods, children can lose their ability to communicate in their mother tongue within two to three years of starting school. They may retain receptive skills in the language but they will use the majority language in speaking with their peers and siblings and in responding to their parents. By the time children become adolescents, the linguistic division between parents and children has become an emotional chasm. Pupils frequently become alienated from the cultures of both home and school, with predictable results.

questions.text:
[Herding] Do the following statements agree with the information given in the text? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
Animals form herds as a way of defending themselves from being attacked.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "as a form of protection against predators" — TRUE — yirtqichlardan himoya

questions.text: Land used by nomadic herders is also suitable for producing a large amount of crops.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "where land is not fertile enough for intensive agricultural farming" — FALSE — yer dehqonchilik uchun yetarlicha unumdor emas

questions.text: Sheep are the most common animals herded by nomadic herders.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "In Africa, nomadic tribes herd various animals such as cattle, goats, sheep and camels" — NOT GIVEN — qaysi hayvon eng ko'p ekani aytilmagan

questions.text: The Fulani people frequently eat the animals which they herd.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "are rarely slaughtered for meat" — FALSE — go'shti uchun kamdan-kam so'yiladi

questions.text: In the tundra, reindeer are generally more valuable than other animals.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "nomads usually herd domesticated reindeer, horses, musk-oxen and yaks" — NOT GIVEN — bug'u qimmatroq degan gap yo'q

questions.text: Animals provide a source of income for nomadic herders.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "they sell their herds’ materials for goods and services, or herd other people’s animals for a fee" — TRUE — hayvonlar daromad manbai

questions.text: Nomadic groups who live in settled communities usually retain their language and customs.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "The unique language and customs of nomads become redundant in settled urban or suburban life" — FALSE — til va urf-odatlar saqlanmaydi

questions.text:
[Semi-nomadic and transhumance herding] Complete the notes below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
Almost all Bedouin are now semi-nomadic because of ___ and oil production.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "recurring drought throughout Western Asia in the 1960s limited fertile areas" — drought

questions.text: Sami have survived by herding, ___ and catching wild animals.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "supplemented by fishing and trapping" — fishing

questions.text: Transhumance takes place in areas which are ___.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "Another type of herding in mountainous regions is called transhumance" — mountainous

questions.text: Transhumance herders stay in permanent ___.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "live in fixed settlements" — settlements

questions.text: ___ have disappeared as a result of transhumance.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "thousands of years of transhumance have transformed forests into grassland" — forests

questions.text: Cattle and sheep spend the ___ in the middle pastures.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "Shepherds lead herds to the middle pastures during the spring" — spring — yozda/kuzda qo'y va qoramol eng baland yaylovda

questions.text:
[Malaria in 19th-century Italy] Complete the summary below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Up until the late nineteenth century, experts failed to make the connection between malaria and ___.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "did not make the further leap towards insects" — insects

questions.text: The most popular belief at the time was the ___ theory, which upheld the idea that diseases were carried by unclean air.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "subscribed to the theory of 'miasma' or 'poisoning of the air'" — miasma

questions.text: Another common idea was that malaria was a ___ disease, and as a result people from certain parts of the country were often held responsible for the spread of epidemics.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "given the widespread belief that malaria was hereditary" — hereditary

questions.text: Malaria was particularly widespread in rural regions, where ___ could be extremely short.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "the life expectancy of land workers was a terrifying 22.5 years" — life expectancy

questions.text:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
The volunteers in Giovanni Battista Grassi's research came from all parts of Italy.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "By releasing mosquitoes into rooms to drink the blood of healthy human volunteers" — NOT GIVEN — ko'ngillilar qayerdan kelgani aytilmagan

questions.text: Experiments in Italy proved that it was possible to remain healthy despite being in malarial zones.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "where healthy people were introduced into malarial zones but kept free of mosquito bites - and remained well" — TRUE

questions.text: In the early twentieth century, quinine was successfully administered to all inhabitants of vulnerable regions.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "peasants were often suspicious of medicine being forced upon them, and doctors were frequently met with hostility and stubborn refusal to accept the treatment offered" — FALSE — hammaga ham berilmadi, ko'pchilik rad etdi

questions.text:
[The conquest of malaria in Italy] Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information?
a figure showing the dramatic results of an anti-malarial drug programme
questions.explanation: Matnda: "Deaths from malaria fell by some 80% in the first decade of the 20th century" — E — 80% raqami

questions.text: an important discovery about how malaria is spread
questions.explanation: Matnda: "the zoologist Giovanni Battista Grassi demonstrated that the micro-organisms causing the disease were carried in the digestive tract of the mosquito" — C — muhim kashfiyot

questions.text: mention of an expert's decision not to halt the spread of the disease
questions.explanation: Matnda: "refused to order the distribution of quinine, so allowing the epidemic to spread unchecked" — F — mutaxassis qarori

questions.text: the significance of the malaria story for today's readers
questions.explanation: Matnda: "Snowden's book also has contemporary relevance" — H — bugungi o'quvchilar uchun ahamiyati

questions.text: examples of false assumptions which held back scientific understanding of malaria
questions.explanation: Matnda: "The consequence of these theories was that little was done to combat the disease before the end of that century" — B — noto'g'ri nazariyalar

questions.text: reference to legislation to support the fight against malaria
questions.explanation: Matnda: "Italy introduced a quinine law and a quinine tax in 1904" — D — qonun

questions.text:
[The significant role of mother tongue language in education] Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
What point is the writer making in the second paragraph?

options.text: Some present studies on children's mother tongues are misleading.
A culturally rich education programme benefits some children more.
Bilingual children can make a valuable contribution to the wealth of a country.
The law on mother tongue use at school should be strengthened.

questions.explanation: Matnda: "To waste the resources of the nation by discouraging children from developing their mother tongues is quite simply unintelligent from the point of view of national self-interest" — C — ikki tilli bolalar mamlakat boyligi

questions.text: Why does the writer refer to something that Goethe said?

options.text: to lend weight to his argument

questions.explanation: Matnda: "strongly support what Goethe, the famous eighteenth-century German philosopher, once said" — A — fikrini kuchaytirish uchun

questions.text: The writer believes that when young children have a firm grasp of their mother tongue

options.text: they can teach older family members what they learn at school.
they go on to do much better throughout their time at school.
they can read stories about their cultural background.
they develop stronger relationships with their family than with their peers.

questions.explanation: Matnda: "children come to school well-prepared to learn the school language and succeed educationally" — B

questions.text: Why are some people suspicious about mother tongue-based teaching programmes?

options.text: They worry that children will be slow to learn to read in either language.
They think that children will confuse words in the two languages.
They believe that the programmes will make children less interested in their lessons.
They fear that the programmes will use up valuable time in the school.

questions.explanation: Matnda: "because they worry that they take time away from the majority language" — D — vaqtni olib qo'yadi

questions.text:
[Bilingual children] Complete the summary using the list of words, A–J.
It has often been noted that bilingual children acquire the ___ to converse in the majority language remarkably quickly.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "pick up conversational skills in the majority language" — I — ability

questions.text: The fact that the mother tongue can disappear at a similar ___ is less well understood.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "how quickly children can lose their ability to use their mother tongue" — D — rate

questions.text: This phenomenon depends to a certain extent on the proportion of people with the same linguistic background that have settled in a particular ___.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "the concentration of families from a particular linguistic group in the neighborhood" — J — area

questions.text: If this is limited, children are likely to lose the active use of their mother tongue, and thus no longer employ it even with ___, although they may still understand it.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "they will use the majority language in speaking with their peers and siblings and in responding to their parents" — F — family

questions.text: It follows that teenage children in these circumstances experience a sense of ___ in relation to all aspects of their lives.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "Pupils frequently become alienated from the cultures of both home and school" — C — dislocation

questions.text:
Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3? Choose YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.
Less than half the children who attend kindergarten in Toronto have English as their mother tongue.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "58% of kindergarten pupils come from homes where English is not the language of communication" — YES — 58% ingliz tilida gaplashmaydi

questions.text: Research proves that learning the host country language at school can have an adverse effect on a child's mother tongue.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "When children continue to develop their abilities in two or more languages throughout primary school, they gain a deeper understanding of language and how to use it effectively" — NO — salbiy emas, aksincha foydali

questions.text: The Foyer programme is to be adopted by the French education system.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "the Foyer program in Belgium, which develops children’s speaking and literacy abilities in three languages (their mother tongue, Dutch and French), most clearly illustrates the benefits of bilingual and trilingual education" — NOT GIVEN — Fransiya qabul qilishi haqida gap yo'q

questions.text: Bilingual children are taught to tell the time earlier than monolingual children.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "Pupils who know how to tell the time in their mother tongue understand the concept of telling time" — NOT GIVEN — kimga ertaroq o'rgatilishi aytilmagan

questions.text: Bilingual children can eventually apply reading comprehension strategies acquired in one language when reading in the other.
questions.explanation: Matnda: "knowing how to distinguish the main idea from the supporting details of a written passage or story, and distinguishing fact from opinion" — YES — o'qish strategiyalari boshqa tilga ko'chadi

sections.title: Writing
sections.content:
Writing Task 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The table and pie charts give information about the total value and sources of fish imported to the US between 1988 and 2000.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

Writing Task 2

You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

Write about the following topic:

Water pollution has become one of the most pressing environmental issues in many parts of the world.

Why is water pollution a growing concern for both individuals and governments?

What measures can be taken to reduce the problem effectively?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
